lesson.title: Centralized by Design: The Client-Server Model
lesson.summary: The client-server model splits network applications into two asymmetric roles, a server that waits and provides a service, and clients that initiate requests to it, centralizing where data and control live.
lesson.body:
Almost every network application has to answer a basic design question: who initiates contact, and who is responsible for what. The client-server model answers it by splitting participants into two clearly different roles. A server sits at a known address, listens for incoming connections, and waits. It does not initiate contact with anyone, its job is to be reachable and to respond. A client is the one that reaches out, it knows or looks up the server's address, initiates the connection, sends a request, and waits for a response. These are not interchangeable roles. A client generally does not accept incoming connections from other clients, and a server generally does not initiate connections to reach out to a client on its own.

This asymmetry is what makes the model centralized. All the shared state, a database, a set of files, the current state of a game world, whatever the application is organized around, lives on the server, in one place or in a small number of coordinated places the server operators control. Every client talks to that same central point, which means the server can maintain a single, consistent, authoritative view of things, and clients never need to know about or coordinate with each other directly. If two clients need to affect the same data, say two users editing the same document, they each do it by talking to the server, and the server is what reconciles the result.

That centralization is also the model's main weakness. Because every client depends on the server being reachable, the server becomes a single point of failure. If it goes down, every client relying on it loses service simultaneously, no matter how many clients there are or how healthy their own machines and networks are. It is also a scaling bottleneck, since the server has to handle load from every client at once, which is exactly the problem that blocking I/O, non-blocking I/O, and epoll or kqueue address, since a server built to serve thousands of simultaneous clients needs an I/O model that does not fall over as connection counts grow.

Despite that weakness, client-server remains the dominant model for most of the applications people use daily, web sites, most APIs, most databases, precisely because centralizing control makes consistency, security, and moderation far easier to reason about than the alternative. The alternative, where there is no single authoritative party and participants deal with each other directly, is the peer-to-peer model, covered next.
